sections.title: RFID products for African markets

Access and ID cards run at 13.56 MHz (global), UHF inlays are tuned to the destination band, and the classic mistake is buying the cheapest generic inlay before fixing band and reader fit. New to frequency planning? Start with our [LF vs HF vs UHF guide](/blog/rfid-frequencies-lf-hf-uhf-explained/), and for credentials see the [access control stack](/solutions/rfid-access-control/).

Country-tuned UHF inlays and labels — ISO/IEC 18000-63 (Gen2) inlays tuned for the destination band (865-868 MHz for most of the continent, 915.4-919 MHz for South Africa) for retail, warehouse, logistics and asset tracking.

sections.title: Get the band right: Africa has no single UHF band
sections.intro: The single most expensive mistake in cross-border RFID sourcing is band mismatch — and Africa makes it easy to get wrong, because there is no one African band. Most of North, East and West Africa mirrors the EU 865-868 MHz band, while South Africa sits roughly 50 MHz higher at 915.4-919 MHz under ICASA. An inlay tuned for Cairo or Nairobi reads short on a Johannesburg portal, and the reverse is just as true. So the rule is simple: name the destination country on the RFQ and the antenna tuning follows it. (Access cards at 13.56 MHz are global and unaffected.) The band table below lists only allocations we can source to a regulator; where a country is not listed, we confirm it with the national regulator before quoting.

sections.title: Landed cost: HS 8523.52, and why the duty line is country-specific
sections.intro: The unit price is the headline; the landed cost is the story — and in Africa that story has a different ending in every country, because duty and VAT depend on the destination and its trade regime. What is constant is the classification; what varies is the rate. Our [RFID RFP template](/blog/rfid-rfp-template-questions-suppliers/) shows the quote-comparison math in full.

dataHighlight.heading: One classification, many national duty rates
dataHighlight.text: RFID cards and inlays commonly classify under HS 8523.52 ("smart cards / media") — that six-digit heading is consistent worldwide. What changes across Africa is the applied duty and VAT: each country sets its own rate and applies its own trade-regime preferences (AfCFTA, plus regional blocs such as ECOWAS, the EAC, SADC and COMESA). So there is no single "African duty rate" — we quote duty and VAT against your specific destination and, where we can settle them, offer DDP so the number you sign is the landed number. Where DDP is not available on a lane, we ship CIF or DAP and your broker clears. Confirm the exact classification and rate with your customs broker.
dataHighlight.source: WCO Harmonized System heading 8523.52; national customs tariffs vary by country

bullets: The HS 8523.52 heading is the constant; the duty and VAT rate is the variable — it is set by the destination country, not the continent.
Ask for the HS 8523.52 line and country-of-origin on the commercial invoice so your broker enters the goods correctly the first time.
DDP availability is confirmed per lane; where it is not offered, CIF or DAP plus your broker is the honest alternative — we will not quote a duty we cannot settle.

sections.title: How an African order runs, step by step
sections.intro: No guesswork on band or border — this is the cadence a first order follows, and it starts by pinning the destination country.

items.text: Send the destination country, the reader make/model, quantity and artwork. The quote comes back with the country's UHF band tuning specified — or, if the country's allocation needs confirming, verified with the national regulator first — and an Incoterm (EXW / CIF / DAP / DDP).

items.text: Cards printed and encoded, or UHF inlays converted and tuned to the destination band; read-tested before packing.

items.label: Delivery

sections.title: Proof an African buyer can verify without a plant visit
sections.intro: Proud Tek supplies integrators, resellers, banks, government agencies and enterprises across Africa — but don't take a market page's word for it. Verify us the way you would audit any China factory: check certificates with the issuing registrar using our [ISO verification guide](/blog/rfid-manufacturer-iso-9001-14001-certification-verification/), then work through the [China factory audit checklist](/blog/china-rfid-factory-audit-checklist/).
checklist: Confirm the destination country's UHF band in writing on the PO — 915.4-919 MHz for South Africa (ICASA), 865-868 MHz for most of the continent — and hold the approved sample as the reference.
Request free samples and read them on your own readers before any bulk order; for UHF, insist the samples are tuned to your country's band, not a generic global inlay.
Ask for the ISO/IEC 14443 (HF cards) and ISO/IEC 18000-63 (UHF inlays) conformance, and for reader-side radio the national type-approval reference for your country.
Get the HS 8523.52 classification and country-of-origin on the proforma, and confirm duty, VAT and DDP availability for your specific destination before you commit.
For high-security or government credentials, specify DESFire EV3 (AES-128) rather than legacy MIFARE Classic.

faq.question: Which UHF frequency band should I order for my African country?
faq.answer: There is no single African band, so the answer is the destination country's allocation. Sourced examples: South Africa uses 915.4-919 MHz (up to 4 W EIRP) under ICASA; Egypt uses 865-868 MHz in four 200 kHz channels at 2 W e.r.p. under the NTRA; Kenya uses the 865-868 MHz band on the EN 302 208 basis under the Communications Authority; Morocco uses 865-868 MHz under the ANRT. If your country is not listed, we confirm the allocation with the national regulator before quoting. HF and NFC cards at 13.56 MHz are global and unaffected.

faq.question: Why can't you just ship one "Africa" UHF tag?
faq.answer: Because the bands differ by roughly 50 MHz across the continent. Most of Africa mirrors the EU 865-868 MHz band, but South Africa runs 915.4-919 MHz — and passive inlay antennas are tuned per band. An EU-tuned 865-868 MHz inlay reads short on a South African 915.4-919 MHz portal, and a South-Africa-tuned inlay reads short in Egypt or Kenya. Specify the destination country and we tune to match; radio physics does not read purchase orders.

faq.question: Are 13.56 MHz access and ID cards the same across Africa?
faq.answer: Yes. HF at 13.56 MHz (MIFARE Classic, DESFire, NFC) is globally harmonised, so one card spec works in every African market — the band split only affects UHF inlays and labels. That is why access control, national ID and banking-credential cards can be standardised continent-wide while UHF asset tags are tuned per country.

faq.question: How do import duty and VAT work for African orders?
faq.answer: RFID cards and inlays commonly classify under HS 8523.52 ("smart cards"), which is consistent worldwide, but the applied duty and VAT are set by the destination country and its trade regime, so there is no single African rate. We quote duty and VAT against your specific destination and offer DDP where the lane allows so the quoted price is the landed price; otherwise we ship CIF or DAP and your broker clears. Confirm the exact classification and rate with your customs broker.

faq.question: Can you deliver RFID products to any African country?
faq.answer: We ship across Africa via DHL, FedEx and UPS express to African capital cities, typically in 5-10 business days, with full export documentation to support customs clearance at the destination port of entry. For bulk programmes we use sea freight to major ports including Lagos, Mombasa, Dar es Salaam, Tema and Durban.

faq.question: Do you offer payment terms for African government projects?
faq.answer: Yes. For government-funded projects with official procurement documentation (purchase orders, Letters of Award) we can structure payment terms including Letter of Credit, deferred payment and milestone-based invoicing, assessed on a project-by-project basis. We also accept T/T wire transfer for standard orders.

faq.question: Can you supply EMV card bodies for African bank card programmes?
faq.answer: We manufacture dual-interface and contactless smart-card bodies with EMV-compatible chips. Full EMV certification is performed by the issuing bank's payment scheme (Visa, Mastercard) during personalisation — we supply the card body with embedded chip ready for your bureau's personalisation and certification process, not the EMV certificate itself.

brief.label: Africa has no single UHF band
brief.text: UHF RFID allocations vary by country across Africa, so a passive inlay must be tuned for the destination. South Africa uses 915.4-919 MHz (FHSS, up to 4 W EIRP) under ICASA; Egypt uses 865-868 MHz in four 200 kHz channels at 2 W e.r.p. under the NTRA; Kenya uses the 865-868 MHz band on the EN 302 208 basis under the Communications Authority; Morocco uses 865-868 MHz (including the 865.6-865.8 MHz channel, 2 W e.r.p.) under the ANRT. That is roughly a 50 MHz spread. HF and NFC cards at 13.56 MHz are global.

brief.label: Compliance varies by country
brief.text: Radio type-approval is national — ICASA (South Africa), NTRA (Egypt), the Communications Authority (Kenya), ANRT (Morocco), NCC (Nigeria) and peers. The reader is the regulated radiator and carries the national approval; passive tags are field devices. Data-protection regimes also differ by country (for example South Africa's POPIA, Kenya's Data Protection Act, Nigeria's NDPA) and are a system concern, not a card-blank one. ISO/IEC 14443 (HF cards) and ISO/IEC 18000-63 (UHF Gen2) are the common air-interface standards.
